hook: NOT ALL STUDENT LOANS ARE EQUAL
youtube_title: Your Lender Calls It a Student Loan. Bankruptcy Law Might Not 🦝⚖️
caption: Bankruptcy Code §523(a)(8) protects specific categories of education debt from discharge. A private loan that fits none of them may be treated like ordinary debt — but many loans do fit, and details decide it.
script: Some student loans can be wiped out in bankruptcy like a credit card. Most can't. [disclaimer] Meet Gary. Gary has student loans, a credit card bill, and no money. He files for bankruptcy. In American bankruptcy, a lot of normal debt, like credit cards, can be wiped out. But most student loans are really hard to wipe out. You usually have to prove paying them would cause a huge hardship. Gary figures that's it. His loans are stuck forever. But the law only protects certain kinds of loans. Ones made or backed by the government or nonprofit programs. School benefits and scholarships. And private loans that meet the tax code's definition of a qualified education loan. Wait. So it depends on the type of loan, not what the lender calls it? You see, it's like a club with a guest list. Calling yourself a VIP doesn't get you in. Being on the list does. A private loan that doesn't fit any group might be treated like a normal debt. Like a credit card. But most federal loans fit. A lot of private loans fit too. In one recent case, the judge said the loans fit, so they were not wiped out. Ask a bankruptcy lawyer. So the question that decides Gary's future isn't how much he owes. It's what kind of loan he signed. [loop] So before you assume every student loan is the same in bankruptcy, remember

script_old: Your lender calls it a student loan, but bankruptcy law may see it differently. In U.S. bankruptcy, most student loans are hard to wipe out. Under the Bankruptcy Code, they're excepted from discharge unless repaying them would impose an undue hardship on the debtor and their dependents. But that protection is defined by categories. One: loans made, insured or guaranteed by a government unit, or under government or nonprofit programs. Two: obligations to repay money received as an educational benefit, scholarship or stipend. Three: any other educational loan that counts as a qualified education loan under the tax code. A recent bankruptcy opinion described that third group as private loans to people attending eligible schools for certain qualified expenses. So the label on the loan isn't the test. The statute's categories are. A private loan that doesn't fit any of them may be treated like other unsecured debt. Here's the limit. Most federal loans, and many private ones, do fit, and then you'd still need to prove undue hardship. In that very opinion, the court found the debtor's loans did qualify, so they weren't discharged. Whether a loan fits depends on its details, so that's a question for a bankruptcy lawyer. [loop] So before you assume every student loan is the same in bankruptcy, remember
